episode.broadcastScript:
This is The Innovation Pulse for Monday, March 16, 2026. Here's what's happening in A.I. and higher education. Faculty at Metropolitan State University Denver are facing challenges with validating online assessments amid the rise of A.I., according to Denver7.

-

In Insights & Trends today, according to Denver7, faculty at Metropolitan State University (MSU) Denver are grappling with issues surrounding student assessment in the A.I. era. Jeff Loats, professor and director of the Center for Teaching, Learning and Design at MSU, noted that validating online assessments has become a significant challenge. He explained, "If assessments are online, we don't know how to do that in a valid way."

Sam Jay, MSU's Executive Director of Online Learning, sees this as a chance to improve assessment practices. Vice Provost Shaun Schafer discussed his approach of switching his journalism class from in-person lectures to online lectures with in-person assignments. He aims to incorporate more case study and application-based assignments, which are harder for A.I. to complete authentically.

Schafer acknowledged the difficulty for instructors to dramatically change teaching methods, highlighting the variance in faculty buy-in, with some allowing limited A.I. use and others restricting it entirely. The challenge remains in creating definitive guidelines across more than 100 majors at MSU, illustrating how institutional responses are still evolving. 

-

Turning to Practical Tips, San Diego Community College District is hosting InnovAItion Day on March 20, according to City Times. The event will feature faculty, staff, and students exploring responsible A.I. use in education. Attendees will participate in student-led panels and discussions focused on the role of A.I. in learning environments.

-

From the Case Study file, Universidad Austral has teamed up with Universidad de La Sabana to develop an intelligent dashboard for student assessment, reports Times Higher Education. This tool allows educators and students to interact with A.I. as both a teammate and teaching assistant. It provides continuous feedback and aids students in honing their judgment when using A.I. technology.

-

Next up, in another Case Study, UNC Greensboro's School of Nursing is actively integrating A.I. into its curriculum, according to UNC Greensboro. Faculty members have been appointed as A.I. Champions to help integrate the technology across different academic areas, including simulation and training. Currently, seventy percent of the faculty are making use of A.I. tools to enhance student engagement and accommodate diverse learning styles.

-

Meanwhile, over at George Washington University, as reported by GW Today, Professor Michael Tadesse is redesigning his marketing courses with a focus on an "innovation mindset lab." In this lab, students collaborate with real businesses to build A.I.-enabled prototypes. This method encourages students to prioritize strategic thinking and adaptation over traditional content delivery.

-

In Practical Tips today, according to Open Source For You, new analysis shows that no-code A.I. tools are broadening access for academic users. These platforms enable students and faculty to leverage A.I. capabilities without requiring programming expertise. Whether utilizing Google Teachable Machine for beginners or more advanced research assistants for conducting literature reviews, these tools are expanding the potential for academic applications of A.I.

-

That's today's Innovation Pulse. Full coverage and source links at innovating higher ed dot com.
